facts.text: On this date in 1920, KDKA in Pittsburgh made the first licensed commercial radio broadcast — covering the Harding-Cox election results. Within three years, 500 stations existed across the US.
On this date in 1947, Howard Hughes flew the Spruce Goose exactly once — a single, mile-long hop over Long Beach Harbor. It never flew again.
Manila is the world's most densely populated city proper, packing over 70,000 people per square kilometer — denser than any borough of New York City by a factor of four.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined, containing roughly 60% of the world's fresh surface water in lake form.
Indonesia spans a wider east-west distance than the continental United States, yet sits entirely within the tropics — its 17,000 islands stretch across three time zones.
On this day in 1936, John Maynard Keynes published 'The General Theory' — a book written partly to save capitalism from itself, which conservatives would spend the next 90 years trying to undo.
On November 2, 1988, the Morris Worm became the first malware to cripple the internet. The damages were estimated at $10M — roughly what a mid-tier trading desk spends on Bloomberg terminals today.
The NYSE's famously chaotic open-outcry trading floor was nearly empty by 2007. What looked like 200 years of tradition was, in practice, theater kept alive for TV cameras.
Saudi Aramco pays more in taxes and royalties to the Saudi government each year than Apple, Microsoft, and Google combined earn in net profit.
Warren Buffett held more U.S. Treasury bills in 2024 than the Federal Reserve. Berkshire's cash pile briefly exceeded $300B — a one-man sovereign wealth fund dressed in Omaha flannel.
On this day in 1988, the Morris Worm became the first malware to spread across the internet, infecting ~6,000 machines. Its creator, Robert Morris, later became an MIT professor.
On this day in 2000, humans began an unbroken streak of living in space aboard the ISS — a streak that has not ended since.
A teaspoon of neutron star material weighs about a billion tons. Gravity there is so extreme that a marshmallow dropped from one meter would hit the surface with nuclear-bomb force.
Your body contains roughly 37 trillion cells, but only about half of them are human. The rest are bacteria, fungi, and other microbes that outnumber your own DNA at every turn.
Light takes 8 minutes to travel from the Sun to Earth, but the photons themselves were generated in the Sun's core up to 100,000 years ago, crawling outward before their final sprint.
On this day in 1936, the BBC launched the world's first regular television service — broadcasting to an audience of roughly 400 TV sets in London.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. The pyramid is that old.
On this day in 1947, Howard Hughes flew the Spruce Goose exactly once — a single 26-second hop over Long Beach harbor that was also its last flight.
The fax machine was invented in 1843, before the telephone. You could fax someone 33 years before you could call them.
Oxford University began teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. When Montezuma was born, Oxford had already been running for 300 years.

Saudade (Portuguese): a melancholic longing for something beloved and lost. Linguists consider it untranslatable — English requires an entire sentence to approximate what Portuguese captures in four syllables.
Apricity: the warmth of winter sun on your skin. The word existed in English by 1623, then quietly vanished from dictionaries, leaving us with no single word for one of winter's finest pleasures.

On this day in 1755, the Lisbon earthquake killed up to 60,000 people — and gave philosophy the word 'optimism' as a pejorative, after Voltaire wrote Candide to mock Leibniz's claim that this is the best of all possible worlds.

On November 2, 1920, KDKA Pittsburgh made the first licensed commercial radio broadcast. The word 'broadcast' was stolen directly from agriculture, where it meant scattering seeds widely across a field.
Hiraeth (Welsh): a homesickness for a home you cannot return to — or that never existed. It folds grief, nostalgia, and longing into one word English has spent centuries failing to invent.
On this date in 2008, Satoshi Nakamoto published the Bitcoin whitepaper to a cryptography mailing list. Nine people received it. None responded with enthusiasm.
On Nov 2, 2022, FTX's on-chain wallets began showing unusual outflows hours before Sam Bankman-Fried publicly denied insolvency. The blockchain logged what PR denied.
Bitcoin's timelock opcode, OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY, sat disabled in the codebase for years before activation in 2015. Satoshi wrote it in but never turned it on.
Ethereum's genesis block contains a hidden message: the hash of a Times headline about bank bailouts — a direct mirror of Bitcoin's own genesis block editorial.
The DAO hack of 2016 didn't steal funds — it legally exploited a recursive call vulnerability. Ethereum's hard fork was the irregular act; the attacker followed the code exactly.

On this date in 2014, Demis Hassabis presented the first DQN paper at a Montreal workshop — a neural net learning Atari from raw pixels. Most attendees didn't realize they were watching the opening move of the modern RL era.

On this date in 1988, the Morris Worm infected roughly 6,000 machines — about 10% of the internet. Its self-replicating logic foreshadowed the adversarial optimization problems that now consume entire AI safety research programs.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed around 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity — comparable to the annual consumption of 4,500 average US homes, for a single model trained once.
The transformer architecture, now running inside almost every major AI product on earth, was published by eight Google researchers in 2017. Three of the eight authors have since left Google.

Chinchilla scaling laws, derived from a 2022 DeepMind paper, showed the entire field had been systematically under-training models relative to dataset size — meaning years of prior compute had been spent in the wrong direction.
